# Cwift.net

> Cwift.net is the minimal, first-person site for Brian Ward's 24-hour desktop appraisals of California homes and condominiums. Brian Ward is a California Certified Residential Real Estate Appraiser (license AR036053) who has appraised California homes since 2004. Reports are emailed within 24 hours of payment and photos, seven days a week. Same appraiser and service as cwift.com; standard-schedule reports are also offered by date-of-death.com.

## Facts
- Within 24 hours: Standard Desktop $675, Basic Desktop $450
- Regular schedule (5–10 business days): Standard $449, Basic $299
- The 24 hours start once payment and photos have both arrived; weekends and holidays count
- Coverage: all of California; single-family homes, condominiums and townhomes (not 2–4 units, apartments, commercial or land); not for loans
- Contact: contact@cwift.net or https://www.cwift.net/order. No phone number by design: email and online submission are the fastest way to get service
- Statement: I've prepared desktop appraisals for every purpose on this list. Some situations still call for an in-person appraisal, though, so check with your attorney or tax advisor first to make sure a desktop report is right for yours.

## Uses (date of death first)
- Date of death & step-up in basis: Heirs usually receive a fresh tax basis equal to the home's value on the day the owner died. The appraisal pins down that figure, so capital gains are calculated correctly when the house sells, even if the death was years ago.
- Trusts & estates: Trustees and executors need a value they can defend: for an accounting, for dividing things fairly, or for selling the house to one of the beneficiaries. A signed appraisal answers the question of where the number came from.
- Divorce & separation: Whether one of you keeps the house or it gets sold, settlement talks move faster with an independent value. I can value the home as of today, the date of separation, or both.
- Family sales & buyouts: Buying out a brother's share, selling to your daughter, or splitting a house with a former partner? The appraisal gives everyone the same starting point and records a fair price.
- Gift tax: Deeding a house, or part of one, to a relative is a gift with a value that gets reported. The appraisal supports the figure on the federal gift-tax return, Form 709.
- Prop 19 transfers: When a parent's home passes to a child, Prop 19 limits how much of the old assessment carries over. Market value on the transfer date shows where you stand with the county assessor.
- Property tax appeals: If the county assesses your home above what it would sell for, an independent appraisal is the evidence for a decline-in-value review or a formal appeal.
- Bankruptcy: Your attorney needs a supportable value for the schedules and the homestead exemption. Problems with the house get documented from your photos, so they count.
- Before you sell: Set the asking price with an opinion from someone who isn't trying to win your listing.
- Before you buy: Paying cash, buying from family, or skipping the appraisal contingency? Check the price while you can still walk away.
- Immigration sponsors (I-864): Sponsors who count home equity on the Affidavit of Support are asked for a recent appraisal by a licensed appraiser. This is that appraisal.
- Bail & property bonds: Courts that take a property bond want proof of the equity, usually from a licensed appraiser. A current report keeps the bond paperwork moving.

## Questions
Q: How fast is 24 hours, really?
A: Your report is emailed no more than 24 hours after I have both your payment and your photos. Saturdays, Sundays and holidays count like any other day.

Q: What do I need to send?
A: The address, what the appraisal is for, the date you need the value for, and photos of the outside and inside. A few lines about recent updates or problems help too.

Q: Do you come out to the house?
A: No. That's what makes it a desktop appraisal, and it's why it can be finished in a day.

Q: Will my CPA, attorney or the IRS accept it?
A: It's a signed appraisal by a California Certified Residential Real Estate Appraiser, prepared under USPAP, the national appraisal standards. I've done desktop appraisals for every purpose on this site, but acceptance is up to whoever receives the report, so check with your advisor if you're unsure.

Q: Can you value a date in the past?
A: Yes. Most date-of-death, divorce and gift appraisals are for past dates. If the house has changed since then, send older photos or describe what's different.

Q: What does it cost?
A: Within 24 hours: $675 for a Standard Desktop or $450 for a Basic Desktop. On the regular 5–10 business-day schedule they're $449 and $299.

Q: Standard or Basic?
A: Both use the same analysis. Standard adds photos, maps, a property description and a market section, which helps when someone else will review the report.

Q: Why can't I call?
A: Because it would slow things down. Email and the form put everything in writing at once, photos included. Write to contact@cwift.net any time.

Q: How do I pay?
A: You'll get a secure invoice by email after I've reviewed your request.

Q: Which properties can you appraise?
A: Single-family homes and condominiums, including townhomes, anywhere in California. Not 2–4 unit buildings, apartment buildings, commercial property or land.

Q: Can I use it to refinance or get a loan?
A: No. Lenders order their own appraisals.

Q: What if the report gets something wrong about my house?
A: Tell me. If I misread a feature or the condition, I'll correct it at no charge.

## Why desktop appraisals are credible
1. The rulebook allows it: Appraisers follow USPAP, the national appraisal standards, and California requires licensed appraisers to comply. USPAP lets the appraiser decide how much inspection an assignment needs, and requires the report to say plainly whether the property was inspected. My desktop reports disclose that, along with what information I relied on.
2. Mortgage companies use them: Fannie Mae's Selling Guide (section B4-1.2-02) allows desktop appraisals, done without a current visit to the home or the comparable sales, for some home-purchase loans. If the method holds up when hundreds of thousands of dollars are being lent against a house, it holds up for an estate, a buyout or a tax return.
3. The IRS list doesn't include a visit: For gift-tax returns, Treasury regulations spell out who may prepare a supporting appraisal and what it has to contain: dates, a description of the property, the method, the information considered and the reasoning. Walking through the house isn't on the list (26 CFR 301.6501(c)-1(f)(3)).
4. Every appraisal is mostly remote: Appraisers judge comparable sales from MLS records, photos and public data without ever going inside them. In a desktop appraisal your home is studied the same way, with better photos, because you took them.
5. Your evidence covers more: A quick walk-through can miss the new roof, the old water damage or the bathroom that hasn't been touched since 1978. Your photos and notes can show all of it, and the report lists what was provided.
6. Someone stands behind it: Every report is signed by me, Brian Ward, California Certified Residential Real Estate Appraiser, license AR036053. You can look the license up on the state's appraiser search. I keep a workfile for every report, and if I misread something about your home I fix it free.
